## Abstract

To date, glial cells in the enteric nervous system have been categorized by spatial location and morphology. Here, Muppirala et al. define distinct subtypes of enteric glia that align with this spatial classification and identify tachykinin signaling as a key mediator of glial diversification and subtype-specific function in intestinal motility.

## INTRODUCTION

Glial cells are essential counterparts to neurons throughout the nervous system, ranging from astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia in the central nervous system (CNS) to satellite glia and Schwann cells in the periphery. The enteric nervous system (ENS) is a major branch of the autonomic nervous system that represents the intrinsic neural networks of the digestive tract. The ENS is estimated to contain several hundred million neurons, organized predominantly into two ganglionated plexuses that regulate digestion, host defense, and survival.1–3 Enteric glia outnumber neurons in the ENS and likely constitute the largest glial population outside the brain. It remains unclear, however, if there are different types of ENS glia and, if so, how they are defined.

Enteric glia arise from vagal neural crest progenitors that colonize the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. These progenitors give rise to both neurons and glia, first in the myenteric plexus (MP), located in the outer muscularis externa, and then the smaller submucosal plexus (SMP), located closer to the gut lumen. Whereas enteric neuronal somas are mostly restricted to ganglia in these two plexuses, glia are distributed across the radial axis of the GI tract within and outside ganglia. Enteric glia exhibit different morphologies along this axis, leading to the current working classification that combines location with morphology: extensively branched ‘‘protoplasmic’’ glia associated with neuronal soma within myenteric ganglia (type I; intraganglionic), elongated ‘‘fibrous’’ glia associated with nerve fiber bundles extending between ganglia (type II; connectives), extraganglionic multipolar glia located mostly in the mucosa (type III), and extraganglionic glia with small central soma and bipolar projections associated with nerve fibers in the muscularis externa (type IV; intramuscular).4,5

Molecular markers such as S100B, SOX10, and PLP1 are shared by most morphological types of enteric glia, while the expression of others, including GFAP and ALDH1L1, is more restricted, hinting at functional heterogeneity.6–8 Consistent with this possibility, glia within even individual ganglia are variably gap junction-coupled and exhibit different calcium responses to stimuli.9–11 More recently, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have unveiled transcriptionally distinct populations of enteric glia in mice and humans.12–17 How these transcriptionally defined populations map onto the spatial-morphological classification remains unclear. Studies have implicated enteric glia in nearly every aspect of GI function, from motility to immunity; however, the manipulations targeted all glial populations, leaving individual contributions unresolved.3,18–20 Moreover, most studies simultaneously targeted other glial populations in the CNS and peripheral nervous system (PNS) because no existing genetic tools are selective for enteric glia. This has made it challenging to isolate the functional significance of enteric glia, overall, much less that of individual subtypes.

Here, we use RNA-seq, genetic labeling, and pharmacology to investigate the transcriptional and functional heterogeneity of glia along the radial axis of the murine small intestine. We define the transcriptomes of mucosal, intramuscular, and intraganglionic glia and identify Tacr3 as a gene enriched within intraganglionic glia that is unique to glia in the ENS. Tacr3 encodes the G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) for the neuropeptide neurokinin B (NKB). We find that the NKB-TACR3 axis is necessary for normal establishment of enteric glial populations during development and later functions to regulate intestinal motility in homeostasis. Together, these findings delineate transcriptionally and functionally distinct populations of enteric glia that can be clearly linked to the spatial-morphological classification, identify genetic approaches to selectively manipulate enteric glia, and establish tachykinin signaling as a key mediator of enteric glial diversification and function.

## RESULTS

### Mucosal and muscularis glia are transcriptionally distinct populations in the small intestine

The laminar structure of the intestine creates markedly different microenvironments for its cellular constituents. The muscular wall contains two orthogonally oriented layers of smooth muscle, with the MP in between. Glia in this muscularis associate with neuronal soma within myenteric ganglia, nerve fiber bundles connecting ganglia, and individual nerve fibers innervating the muscle. Glia in the mucosa associate with nerve fibers but also appose epithelial, vascular, and immune cells. We reasoned that glia in these two microenvironments were most likely to be different subtypes. Few studies have directly compared muscularis and mucosal glia, but evidence suggests they respond differently to perturbations, such as the absence of microbiota21 or lipopolysaccharide exposure.22

To assess their differences, we developed a method to rapidly separate the mucosal and muscularis compartments in the mouse ileum and isolate constituent glia for transcriptional profiling (Figure 1A).23 Application of this method to dual reporter mice in which glia were labeled with green fluorescent protein (GFP) and intestinal epithelial cells were labeled with tdTomato (Vil1Cre Rosa26tdTomato/+ Plp1eGFP mice), confirmed that the two compartments were well partitioned (Figure S1A). We applied this approach to small intestinal segments from 8- to 12-week-old Plp1eGFP mice to isolate mucosal and muscularis glia in tandem for bulk RNA-seq (Figure S1B). Unbiased hierarchical clustering revealed that transcriptional profiles segregated first by laminar compartment and then by presence or absence of GFP (Figures S1C and S1D), indicating influences of the microenvironment and glial identity.

Differential analysis of gene expression in cells from both compartments identified Plp1 and Kcnj10 among the top five enriched genes in GFP+ glia (Figure 1B), consistent with broad enteric glial expression.6,25 GFP+ cells in both compartments were also enriched for other characteristic enteric glial genes, including Sox10, Gfap, and S100b (Figure S1E), indicating effective glial isolation. Despite this shared glial identity, mucosal and muscularis glia differed in their transcriptional signatures (Figure 1B; Table S2). Unexpectedly, mucosal glia were enriched for transcripts characteristic of macrophages, such as Cx3cr1, Mpeg1, Adgre1, Cd300a, and Csf1r26,27 (Figure 1C). BayesPrism deconvolution analysis using scRNA-seq data from intestinal mucosa indicated selective similarity of the GFP+ transcriptome to that of macrophages rather than to more abundant cell types, such as epithelial cells (Figure S1F), arguing against general mucosal contamination.28 Furthermore, in dual reporter mice in which Plp1+ glia were labeled with tdTomato and Cx3cr1+ cells were labeled with GFP (Plp1CreERT2 Rosa26tdTomato/+ Cx3cr1GFP/+), Mpeg1, Adgre1, Csf1r, and Cd300a transcripts were all detected in subsets of mucosal glia in situ (Figures 1D, 1E, and S1G). Notably, Csf1r was expressed by more than 10% of mucosal Plp1+ cells, whereas GFP and tdTomato reporter expression were mutually exclusive, indicating that mucosal glia do not express Cx3cr1 in situ.

Given evidence for some shared gene expression between macrophages and mucosal glia, we performed two parallel analyses of the mucosal glia transcriptome, one with untransformed data and the other correcting for Cx3cr1, Mpeg1, and Adgre1 expression in GFP+ cells, as they were detected broadly across macrophages but in the least number of mucosal glia (Figure 1E). Differential gene analysis using this correction recapitulated in situ hybridization data, with Cx3cr1 no longer emerging as a differentially expressed gene, while Csf1r, Cd300a, and Mpeg1 remained mildly enriched (Figure S1G). Sox10 and Cdh19 were enriched in GFP+ cells post correction, which aligned with in situ hybridization showing these transcripts restricted to mucosal and muscularis glia (Figure S1H). Nevertheless, the correction was too stringent because S100b, Adgre1, and Tarm1 dropped below the threshold for significance despite detection in mucosal glia (Figure S1H). Therefore, we use both unmodified and high-stringency transcriptomes for mucosal glia for downstream analyses (Table S2).

Mucosal glia shared 460 (unmodified) or 94 genes (high stringency) with muscularis glia, which were uniquely expressed compared with surrounding GFP− cells, contributing to a core glial identity. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using g:Profiler for biological processes29 revealed mucosal glia to be enriched for immune-related functions, including antigen presentation and leukocyte activation (Figure 1F), previously attributed broadly to Sox10+ enteric glia.30 Muscularis glia were enriched for genes associated with neurogenesis, a glial capability triggered by specific perturbations in vivo.31,32 These observations suggest that previously reported enteric glial functions may be divided among compartment-specific subtypes.

Enteric glia share a developmental lineage with Schwann cells,33 molecular and morphological features of astrocytes,8,34 and transcriptional programs with myelinating glia.6 To determine whether this hybrid identity results from enteric glia in different compartments being analogous to distinct types of extraintestinal glia, we analyzed glial cell gene signatures from scRNA-seq datasets of the brain and peripheral nerves (Table S3).12,24 GSEA of these signatures in our muscularis and high-stringency mucosal glial transcriptomes revealed mucosal glia to be highly similar to microglia, whereas muscularis glia most closely resembled satellite glia and astrocytes (Figure 1G). Both populations were equivalently similar to non-myelinating Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes. Together, the transcriptional profiles of mucosal and muscularis glia indicate that neither are directly analogous to extraintestinal glia but are biologically distinct from each other, with niche-specific features.

### Tacr3 expression distinguishes intraganglionic glia of the MP

Next, we focused on identifying compartment-specific functions and molecular markers of muscularis glia that could enable selective genetic access. Eight of the 12 genes most enriched in GFP+ cells were more abundant in muscularis than mucosal glia (Figure 2A). Among these, Tacr3 emerged as a strong candidate for an ENS- and compartment-specific glial marker. Tacr3 encodes a GPCR that we previously reported as a glial transcript6 and has been linked to intestinal motor function.35,36 Tacr3 transcripts were enriched in the muscularis layer compared with the mucosa in wild-type mice and diminished upon genetic ablation of Plp1+ glia (Figure S2A),18 supporting compartment-specific expression that is glial dependent. In cross-sections of small intestine, Sox10 transcripts were broadly detectable in S100B-immunoreactive cells, while Tacr3 transcripts were confined to Sox10+/S100B+ cells in the muscularis (Figure S2B).

Previous studies using immunohistochemistry (IHC) ascribed intestinal TACR3 expression to neurons, not glia.37,38 With IHC, we observed clear evidence of TACR3 expression in Plp1+ cells in the MP (Figure 2B) but could not resolve the degree of non-glial expression. To investigate this, we genetically labeled all Tacr3-expressing cells and their progeny utilizing knockin Tacr3IRES-Cre/+ mice. In the hypothalamus of Tacr3IRES-Cre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice (hereafter Tacr3tdTomato), Tacr3 transcripts colocalized with tdTomato in neurons of the arcuate nucleus (Figure S2C), a well-established site of Tacr3 expression.39 In the intestine, Tacr3 was expressed in the MP in juveniles (3 weeks) and adults (8–12 weeks), exclusively within tdTomato+ cells (Figure S2D). To resolve enteric glial and neuronal tdTomato expression, we performed whole-mount IHC of small intestinal and colonic segments from Tacr3tdTomato mice for the pan-glial marker S100B and the pan-neuronal marker ANNA-1. We quantified tdTomato colocalization with glial and neuronal subpopulations in the ENS across the radial axis (Figures 2C–2F). In the muscularis, the majority of intraganglionic glia of the small and large intestines were tdTomato+ (>85% in juveniles and >98% in adults), while virtually all intramuscular glia were tdTomato− (Figures 2E, S2E, and S2F). A minority of S100B+ glia within submucosal ganglia and interganglionic connectives between myenteric ganglia were also genetically labeled, and these proportions modestly increased from 3 to 12 weeks of age (Figures 2E and S2F). TdTomato expression in intramuscular and mucosal glia was rare, even in adult mice (Figures S2E and S2F), indicating that few glia in these compartments expressed Tacr3 or derived from Tacr3-expressing cells. Few neurons were tdTomato+ in the MP and even less in the SMP (Figures 2F, S2E, and S2G). Altogether, qPCR, in situ hybridization, IHC, and genetic labeling identified intraganglionic muscularis glia as the major and relatively specific site of Tacr3 expression throughout the intestine.

To assess Tacr3 expression in extraintestinal glia, we examined intestine, dorsal root ganglia (DRG), sciatic nerve, and brain tissues from Plp1eGFP Tacr3tdTomato dual reporter mice. In the intestine, almost all GFP+ cells within myenteric ganglia colocalized with tdTomato (Figure S3A). In contrast, GFP+ cells in DRG and sciatic nerves did not express tdTomato, consistent with the lack of Tacr3 transcripts in satellite glia and Schwann cells (Figures S3B and S3C).12,24 In the brain, tdTomato did not colocalize with GFP (oligodendrocytes), GFAP (astrocytes), or IBA1 (microglia; Figure S3D). These observations establish that, among glia, Tacr3 is uniquely expressed in the ENS and uncover a genetic tool that enables manipulation of a large population of enteric glia without perturbing major glial populations elsewhere in the nervous system.

### TACR3 signaling activates myenteric glia to regulate intestinal motility

Virtually all intraganglionic glia in the mature MP express TACR3, suggesting that its signaling could be important for subtype-specific functions. Activation of other Gq-coupled receptors in enteric glia, such as those for ATP, increase intracellular Ca2+ in vitro.40 In explants, similar glial Ca2+ responses are seen upon electrical or mechanical activation of colonic migrating motor contractions (CMMCs), a propulsive motor behavior dependent on neuronal activity.41 To determine whether TACR3 is functionally active in a subtype-specific manner, we examined glial Ca2+ responses in Kir4.1CreER Rosa26GCaMP6f/+ mice. Kcnj10, which encodes Kir4.1, is highly expressed by enteric glia (Figure 1B), and Kir4.1CreER mice exhibit Cre-dependent transgene expression in all muscularis glial populations, including intraganglionic, intramuscular, and connectives.25 In explants from these mice, stimulation of the mucosa distal to the imaging field in the mid-colon, evoked a large Ca2+ response in all muscularis glia that trailed the onset of the concomitantly evoked motor contraction by several seconds (Figures 3A and 3B; Video S1). Intraganglionic glia responded first, followed by connective and intramuscular glia. TACR3 inhibition with fezolinetant (1 μM) markedly reduced the number of intraganglionic glia exhibiting Ca2+ responses to these contractions, with a milder effect on connective glia and no effect on intramuscular glia (Figures 3A–3C; Video S2). In the glia that still exhibited Ca2+ responses to contractions in the presence of fezolinetant, response amplitudes were reduced, but onset and duration were unaffected (Figure 3C; Table S1). Conversely, in the absence of evoked contractions, the TACR3 agonist senktide (10 μM) elicited sustained Ca2+ responses in intraganglionic and connective glia but no responses in intramuscular glia (Figures S4A and S4B; Videos S3 and S4). Thus, TACR3 signaling is restricted to specific myenteric glial subtypes and important for their Ca2+ responses during neurogenic contractions, suggesting that this glial GPCR might regulate gut motility.

Glial Ca2+ responses can either stimulate or inhibit colonic contractions, depending on the intracellular pathways and neural circuits engaged.18,19,42 To determine how TACR3 signaling affects intestinal motility in vivo, we administered fezolinetant (10 mg/kg) or vehicle once to wild-type mice and measured total GI transit time and 60-min fecal pellet output (FPO), which typically reflects colonic motor function. GI transit times were faster in fezolinetant-treated males and females (Figures 3D and S4C) and FPO was correspondingly increased (Figure S4D). Conversely, administration of the TACR3 agonist senktide (5 mg/kg) markedly slowed GI transit time and decreased FPO by 67% in males (Figures 3E and S4F). Senktide similarly slowed GI transit in females but did not alter FPO (Figures 3E, S4E, and S4F). Overall, across both sexes, activating and inhibiting TACR3 signaling slowed or accelerated intestinal transit times, respectively, indicating that this signaling pathway dynamically regulates gut motor activity in vivo. To determine whether this is attributable to gut-intrinsic TACR3 signaling, we studied colonic contractions in preparations that enable visualization of propulsive CMMCs along the full length of the colon ex vivo (Figure S4G). Blocking TACR3 signaling in these preparations increased the frequency and velocity of CMMCs and diminished the duration of each contraction (Figures 3F and 3G), consistent with the faster transit times observed in fezolinetant-treated mice in vivo (Figure 3D). In total, these observations support that myenteric glia modulate GI motor behaviors in a TACR3-dependent manner.

### Genetic labeling of Tacr3 expression resolves spatially and transcriptionally distinct populations of muscularis glia

The subtype-specific role of glial TACR3 signaling in gut motility and reports of neurogenic myenteric glia15,16 suggest that spatial location may be linked to functional specialization. Extraganglionic muscularis glia along nerve fibers were virtually all Tacr3− by IHC and genetic labeling (Figures 2B, 2E, and S2F). Accordingly, in Plp1eGFP Tacr3tdTomato dual reporter mice, these intramuscular glia were GFP+ but tdTomato− (Figure 4A). This observation enabled us to leverage genetic labeling to test whether transcriptional segregation correlated with spatial origin. We performed scRNA-seq on GFP+ cells from the small intestinal muscularis of Plp1eGFP Tacr3tdTomato mice at postnatal day 21 (P21), when muscularis glial populations are well established21 (Figures 4A and 4B). 9,878 Plp1+ cells segregated into eight clusters with robust expression of Plp1, S100b, and Sox10, supporting their glial identity (Figures 4C and 4D). The small cluster 6 was enriched for Schwann cell markers, including Mpz and Reln,43 suggesting that the cells originated from gut-extrinsic mesenteric nerves (Figure 4D). Consistent with this possibility, we found that a gene enriched in this cluster, Lgr5, was expressed by Schwann cells in mesenteric and sciatic nerves but absent in gut-intrinsic glia (Figure S5A). Thus, we concluded that the remaining seven clusters represented transcriptionally distinct types of enteric glia (Table S4).

To learn whether spatial origin correlated with transcriptional identity, we examined tdTomato expression. TdTomato transcripts were detected in clusters 2 and 5, which genetic labeling indicated to originate from myenteric ganglia (Figure 2D). Overlapping Tacr3 transcripts in these cells confirmed constitutive Tacr3 expression (Figure 4E), consistent with IHC and in situ hybridization data (Figures 2B and S2D). The smaller cluster 5 was enriched for mitochondrial genes, likely reflecting a stressed state of cluster 2 cells.45 Clusters 0, 3, and 4 exhibited minimal Gfap and Entpd2 expression (Figure 4D), consistent with likely being intramuscular glia, which lack these markers.6,15 Cluster 1 was Gfap+ and Entpd2+ but had limited to no expression of Tacr3 or tdTomato. We concluded that these glia were likely from interganglionic connectives. Cluster 7 was enriched for proliferation genes (Top2a, Lmnb1, and Ccnb1; Figure S5B) but lacked Tacr3 expression, representing either rare tdTomato− myenteric glia or a proliferative extraganglionic muscularis population. The major Tacr3+ cluster, in contrast, was enriched for genes characteristic of quiescence, including Tgfb2, Junb, and Mapk3,46 and hypoxia pathways associated with cell differentiation47 (Figure S5B).

To further define enteric glial heterogeneity, we focused on the 5 largest clusters (clusters 0–4) (Figure 4F). Molecular markers emerged that could be used individually or in combination to distinguish intraganglionic (Cpe and Tacr3), connective (Sfrp1), and intramuscular glia (Pappa and Aldh1a1) (Figures 4G–4J and S5C). Marker expression stratified along an intraganglionic to extraganglionic axis (Figures S5C and S5D), with some programs shared by all muscularis glia while others were restricted to only those within or outside the plexus. Notably, intraganglionic and intramuscular glia segregated from each other, suggesting that they are functionally distinct. Intraganglionic glia were enriched for Cpe and Ramp1 (Figure S5D), which are expressed by enteric glia at P14 that exhibit chromatin accessibility at transcription factors important for neuronal differentiation.15 Putative intramuscular glia were distinguished by expression of Pappa. In small intestines from Plp1eGFP mice, Pappa transcripts were evident in intramuscular, but not myenteric, GFP+ cells that expressed Sox10 (Figure 4I). To further test cluster assignment, we compared the intramuscular glial transcriptome to data from 3,999 glia isolated from the human colonic muscularis following MP depletion, which would leave intramuscular glia.44 Like in mice, human intramuscular glia broadly expressed PLP1, CDH19, and S100B but virtually no GFAP (Figures S5E and S5F). They also widely expressed PAPPA but not TACR3 (Figure 4K).

Collectively, these findings establish that intraganglionic glia in the MP constitutively express Tacr3 and that genetic labeling of Tacr3-expressing cells enables transcriptional identification of populations of enteric glia that correlate with specific spatial-morphological types. This genetic-spatial profiling approach reveals the diversity of glia in the muscularis layer, identifies molecular markers to distinguish different types, and indicates that intraganglionic and intramuscular glia are the most biologically distinct.

### Postnatal TACR3 signaling is necessary for the normal development and diversification of enteric glia

ENS neurogenesis requires downregulating Sox10, while gliogenesis, similar to the extraintestinal PNS, requires maintaining Sox10.43 The lack of Tacr3 expression or genetic labeling in extraintestinal Plp1+ glia hints that Tacr3 is turned on late in gliogenesis in a program unique to the ENS. Analysis of published scRNA-seq data48 of ENS cells from the mouse small intestine at embryonic day 18.5 showed expression of Plp1, Sox10, and S100b in glial progenitors but not Tacr3 (Figure S6A). Tacr3 transcripts were highly enriched in intraganglionic glia by the time of weaning (Figure 4E), suggesting that the onset of expression must occur in the first 3 postnatal weeks. In Tacr3tdTomato mice, although S100B+ cells were abundant in the MP at P1, tdTomato expression was sparse (Figure 5A). From P7 onward, there was a progressive increase in Tacr3 expression such that by P21, over 85% of myenteric glia marked by S100B were tdTomato+ in the small and large intestines, with mild sex differences in timing (Figures 5A and 5B).

The developmental emergence of Tacr3 expression is coincident with glial colonization of tissue compartments outside myenteric ganglia,21 raising the possibility that TACR3 signaling plays a role in this process. To test this possibility, we blocked TACR3 signaling in mice from P14 to P20 and assessed the effects on the small intestinal ENS. Mice were administered the TACR3 antagonist SB2222–00 (5 mg/kg) or vehicle once daily, replicating a paradigm validated in hypothalamic neurons.49 Blocking TACR3 signaling for just 7 days caused a dramatic change in ENS structure, with 54.3% fewer intramuscular glia compared with vehicle-treated mice (Figures 5C and 5D). There was no such effect on the proportions of S100B+ glia within the MP; however, there were phenotypic changes with increased GFAP (Figure 5D). Whereas muscularis glia were disrupted by TACR3 blockade, mucosal glia appeared morphologically intact and undepleted (Figures 5D and S6B). Neurons appeared normal and their density was unchanged in both the MP and SMP (Figure 5E). To determine whether the loss of S100B+ intramuscular glia reflected fewer glia or loss of S100B marker expression, we administered SB2222–00 or vehicle to Plp1eGFP mice from P14 to P20 and compared GFP and S100B expression. GFP+ intramuscular cells were similarly depleted by TACR3 inhibition (Figure S6C). Blocking TACR3 in wild-type mice from P56 to P62, when the ENS is already mature, had no effect on the density of intramuscular or other glia populations (Figures S6D and S6E), showing that TACR3 signaling is required for enteric glial development but not maintenance.

### NKB is necessary for developmental diversification of enteric glia

The high affinity ligand for TACR3 is NKB, a secreted neuropeptide encoded by the Tac2 gene.38 To determine whether NKB-TACR3 signaling regulates enteric glial development, we examined the ENS in 3-week-old Tac2 knockout (KO) mice. In the small intestines of Tac2 KO mice, there were 43.7% fewer S100B+ intramuscular glia than in wild-type littermate controls, a minor decrease in the proportion of S100B+ cells within myenteric ganglia, and no difference in the connectives or mucosa (Figures 6A and 6B). Further phenocopying inhibitor-treated wild-type mice, glia in the MP of Tac2 KO mice showed dysregulation of GFAP expression (Figure 6A). Myenteric neurons were slightly reduced in number and submucosal neurons were again unaffected (Figure 6C). Taken together, our findings indicate that NKB-TACR3 signaling is necessary for normal development and diversification of glia in the ENS, uncovering one of the first molecular pathways to be identified in this process.

NKB has been predominantly studied in the CNS, where it mediates signaling between neurons in circuits modulating thermoregulation, pubertal timing, and fear learning. In the gut, NKB expression was previously reported in enteric neurons in the rat intestine by IHC and in isolated nerve fibers in the mouse colon by genetic labeling.50,51 To identify NKB-expressing cells that could signal to TACR3-expressing myenteric glia, we examined Tac2Cre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice. A small number of tdTomato+ enteric neurons were identified in the MP that branched extensively throughout the muscularis layer to project to multiple myenteric ganglia (Figure 6D) but never to the mucosa. These Tac2+ neurons were marked by the expression of calretinin (CALB2) and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (vAChT; Figures 6E and S7A). A subset of tdTomato+ nerve fibers colocalized with Substance P (Figure S7B), indicating that at least some Tac2+ neurons express multiple tachykinins. These data suggest that Tac2+ cholinergic enteric neurons are the likely source of NKB to TACR3+ enteric glia.

Our observations linking NKB-TACR3 signaling in the muscularis compartment to glial diversification and neuromuscular function in mice raise the possibility that genotype-dependent modulation of this pathway may affect gut motility in humans. We studied single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) from the TACR3 and TAC3 (encodes human NKB) loci for (1) association with frequency of hard stool (reflects stool consistency, a known proxy for colonic transit and constipation52) in 153,185 UK Biobank (UKB) participants with Digestive Health Questionnaire (DHQ) data available and (2) the presence of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) using data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Portal.53 Although no association was detected for TACR3, multiple TAC3 SNPs associated with both more frequent hard stool and higher TAC3 mRNA expression in human esophageal muscularis tissue (Figure 6F). These observations are consistent with our finding of slowed GI transit upon TACR3 activation in mouse models and support a role for this signaling axis in ENS regulation of human gut motility.

## DISCUSSION

In summary, we find that muscularis and mucosal glia are distinct populations of enteric glia that can be distinguished based on Tacr3 expression. Within the muscularis compartment, Tacr3 predominates within intraganglionic glia and can be used to transcriptionally define glial populations that align with the historical spatial-morphological classification of enteric glia. Glial TACR3 signaling is unique to the ENS, where it mediates the developmental diversification of glia in the postnatal period and then regulates glial activity in a subtype-specific manner to tune intestinal motility (Figure S7C).

Enteric glia were initially considered Schwann cells and then later considered gut astrocytes, with neither attribution fully explaining their morphologies, functions, or transcriptional phenotypes. By comparing Plp1+ enteric glia from two different compartments of the small intestine, we found that mucosal and muscularis glia are not just transcriptionally distinct, they resemble different types of extraintestinal glia. Tacr3 was selectively enriched within ganglia in the muscularis, enabling us to explore glial diversity in this compartment with even greater spatial precision. Utilizing scRNA-seq of Plp1eGFP Tacr3tdTomato dual reporter mice, we generated a spatial atlas for glia in the muscularis that defines transcriptional profiles and molecular markers for intramuscular glia and the two types of glia within the MP (intraganglionic and connectives). Whereas some genes were broadly expressed by all muscularis glia (Kcna1 and Cdh19), others were selectively enriched in the MP (Ramp1 and Cpe) or in individual populations such as intraganglionic (Tacr3 and Otor) or intramuscular glia (Pappa and Aldh1a1). Glia in the connectives lacked unique markers; their location in the midst of the intra- to extraganglionic axis may make them less distinct. In addition to linking spatial location with transcriptional identity, our data provide a resource for probing the biology of enteric glial subtypes in the nervous system. A recent scRNA-seq study similarly found segregation between transcriptional signatures of human intra- and extraganglionic enteric glia.17 Although individual molecular markers may differ between species, the combined observations suggest that transcriptional diversity corresponding to spatial location is a conserved property of enteric glia.

Tacr3 expression not only marks a major population of enteric glia but also is important for normal development of ENS glia through signaling by its encoded GPCR. The molecular mechanisms mediating enteric glial development are poorly understood.43 Embyronic Sox10+ ENS progenitors generate both neurons and glia, and individual progenitors give rise to glia at all locations along the radial axis of the small intestine.54 Mucosal glia emerge in the postnatal period in mice and appear to be continuously replaced by progenitors in the MP.21 The development of intramuscular glia is less defined. Genetic labeling revealed that Tacr3 expression emerges in the postnatal period to mark virtually all intraganglionic glia in the MP and a subset in the connectives. Intramuscular and mucosal glia were rarely labeled, indicating that these extraganglionic glia developmentally diverge from Tacr3+ cells. Genetic or pharmacological disruption of NKB-TACR3 signaling, however, selectively depleted Tacr3− intramuscular glia. These findings establish tachykinin signaling as a mediator of enteric glial diversification and suggest that it functions non-cell autonomously. The underlying mechanisms, possibly through modulation of neuronal activity, cell migration, or repulsive cues, remain to be defined.

Mature intraganglionic glia maintain TACR3 expression, which plays roles beyond development. Acute TACR3 inhibition with fezolinetant reduced neurogenic contraction-associated calcium responses in intraganglionic glia ex vivo and accelerated intestinal transit in vivo, indicating that the signaling pathway is tonically active and necessary for normal motor function. Previous studies showed that NKB or the TACR3 agonist senktide could stimulate or inhibit intestinal contractions in rats or guinea pigs, depending on dosage.35,55–57 The effects were presumed to be from TACR3 expression in afferent neurons of the ENS.37,58–60 Our data reveal that glia are the major TACR3-expressing cells in the ENS and that TACR3 signaling, whether to glia, neurons, or both, acts as a brake on motility. Given that glial TACR3 expression is unique to the ENS, this system provides an opportunity to explore how glial neuropeptide signaling alters neuronal function.

Elucidating the biology of intestinal TACR3 signaling has direct relevance to human health. Fezolinetant, the antagonist utilized in our motility experiments, was recently approved for treatment of hot flashes in menopausal women.61 Diarrhea was a side effect in clinical trials.62,63 Our study identifies enteric glia as an un-anticipated target of this medication and uncovers a likely mechanism of action for its adverse effects. Conversely, gut-restricted agonism or antagonism of TACR3 signaling could be useful for slowing or stimulating intestinal motility, respectively, in clinical conditions such as diarrhea and constipation. Chronic use, however, should be considered with caution because ligand knockout was associated with ENS deficits.

Altogether, our observations provide new insights into the functional heterogeneity of enteric glia and propose that mucosal, intraganglionic, and intramuscular glia should be considered distinct types of glia in the ENS. We identify Tacr3 as a molecular marker enriched in intraganglionic glia in the MP that enables genetic access to a major population of enteric glia without affecting other glial cells outside the gut. Finally, we establish tachykinin signaling to glial TACR3 as an important mediator of ENS development and intestinal function, with relevance to human health.

### Limitations of the study

Our transcriptional atlas of enteric glia includes mucosal glia and at least 3 populations of muscularis glia. Because we used bulk RNA-seq for our initial compartment-specific analysis and scRNA-seq for the subsequent muscularis study, the mucosal glial transcriptome cannot be directly compared with the transcriptomes of individual muscularis types. Future spatial transcriptomics studies may enable direct comparisons. We focused on spatial localization rather than morphology because morphological types I, II, and IV can be reasonably assigned to intraganglionic, connective, and intramuscular glia, respectively. Type III glia, however, are found in muscularis and mucosal compartments, and not all mucosal glia exhibit type III morphology. Genetic tools specific to subsets may enable better definition of how transcriptional identity corresponds to morphology. Finally, our motility studies utilized pharmacological agonism and antagonism of TACR3. Thus, they cannot exclude contributions from TACR3+ neurons and leave unresolved the question of whether NKB is the ligand relevant to intestinal motility. Conditional genetic models could address these questions.

## STAR★METHODS

### EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND STUDY PARTICIPANT DETAILS

#### Mice

Mice were housed in a specific pathogen-free facility with a 12-h dark cycle and handled per protocols approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committees of Boston Children’s Hospital or University of Nevada – Reno, adherent to the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Drinking water and laboratory chow were provided ad libitum. Male and female mice were used for most experiments except where noted. Tacr3IRESCre-GFP/+ mice were generated by Richard Palmiter and provided by Victor Navarro (Brigham and Women’s Hospital). The originating investigator reported that the GFP reporter in this line is not detectable and we confirmed this to be the case. Of note, we observed this line to have intermittent Cre activity in the germline. In parent crosses for generation of Tacr3IRESCre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ reporter mice, we observed that ∼50% of pups exhibited broad, nonselective recombination when the Cre allele was present in the male parent and ∼25% of pups when the Cre was present on the female parent. These pups were excluded from analyses. Tac2Cre/+ mice (knockin/knockout Cre allele) were generated by Qiufu Ma and provided by Yi Zhang (Harvard Medical School). Tac2Cre/Cre mice were studied as Tac2 KO. All strains were bred as heterozygotes on a C57BL/6 (JAX 000664) background, unless stated otherwise. For single-cell profiling experiments, Plp1eGFP Tacr3IRESCre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ dual reporter mice were generated by first crossing Plp1eGFP hemizygous mice to Tacr3IRESCre/+ heterozygotes. Female Plp1eGFP Tacr3IRESCre/+ mice were then bred with Rosa26tdTomato/tdTomato homozygous males to generate dual reporter mice. For Plp1CreERT2 Rosa26tdTomato/+ Cx3cr1GFP/+ glia-macrophage dual reporter mice, Plp1CreERT2 Cx3cr1GFP/+ intermediates were generated and then bred with Rosa26tdTomato/tdTomato males. Wild-type CD1 male (>30g) and female (>25g) adult mice were purchased and used for all in vivo pharmacology experiments. Kir4.1CreERT2 mice25 were bred with Rosa26GCaMP6f/GCaMP6f mice to generate Kir4.1CreERT2 Rosa26GCaMP6f/+ mice (referred to as Kir4.1-GCaMP6f mice). Male and female Kir4.1-GCaMP6f mice received tamoxifen-containing food for 7 days at 6 weeks of age to induce Cre activity and were used for imaging at 8–12 weeks of age. Gene expression data were pooled across sexes and not sufficiently powered to quantitatively assess sex as a biological variable; however, expression levels appeared qualitatively similar. The exception was the study of developmental onset of Tacr3 expression, which was adequately powered to examine sex as a variable and revealed a minor sex-associated difference (Figure 5B). For motility experiments, males and females were evaluated separately, without direct comparison of sex-specific effects of TACR3 inhibition or activation. Thus, both sexes were well represented in our studies but the potential for sex-dependent variation remains a limitation when generalizing some findings.

### METHOD DETAILS

#### Immunohistochemistry

For IHC of intestinal cross-sections, mouse tissues were isolated, fixed and stained as previously detailed.6 In brief, intestinal segments were isolated, cut into ∼2 cm segments, and gently rocked in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA)/phosphate buffered saline (PBS) solution at 4°C for 1.5 h. Tissues were then washed with PBS, transferred to 30% sucrose in PBS to equilibrate for 24 h at 4°C, submerged in Sakura OCT medium in embedding molds, and frozen on dry ice. Frozen 10–14-μm tissue sections of duodenum, ileum, and colon were collected on glass slides (Fisherbrand Superfrost), washed for 5 min in PBS, and then incubated in blocking solution (0.1% Triton + 5% heat-inactivated goat serum in PBS) for 1 h in a humidified chamber. Slides were washed 3 × 5 min in PBS and then incubated overnight (∼16 h) at 4°C in primary antibody + blocking solution (see section below for primary antibodies). Slides were washed 3 × 5 min in PBS and incubated for 1.5 h at room temperature (RT) in secondary antibody + DAPI (2 μg/mL). Slides were again washed with PBS and mounted in Vectashield (Vector Labs H-1200). Imaging was done on confocal microscopes at the BCH and Harvard Imaging cores (Zeiss LSM 880, Zeiss LSM 700, and Nikon W1 spinning disk). For whole-mount IHC, mouse tissues were isolated, fixed and stained as previously detailed.6 In brief, small and large intestinal segments from mice were isolated and flushed with cold PBS. Approximately 2-cm sections of ileum and colon were subsequently trimmed, cut along the mesenteric border, and pinned flat on Sylgard plates. Samples were then fixed in freshly thawed 4% PFA for 1.5 h at 4°C and then thoroughly rinsed with PBS. Tissue segments were then incubated in Rabbit anti S100B and Human anti ANNA-1 in blocking buffer (5% HINGS, 20% DMSO, 0.5% PBS Triton) for 48 h at RT. Samples were then washed with 0.5% PBST (6 × 20 min) at RT and incubated for 24 h with Goat anti Rabbit 488 and Goat anti human 647.

Primary antibodies for IHC were used at the given concentrations: polyclonal rabbit anti-GFP (1:1000) chicken anti mCherry (1:500), goat anti IBA1 (1:500), human anti ANNA-1 (1:80,000), rabbit anti HuC/D (1:500), rabbit anti S100B (1:1 Agilent), and chicken anti GFAP (1:1000), rabbit anti VACHT (1:500), rabbit anti Substance P (1:1000), rabbit anti TACR3 (1:1000), rabbit anti ALDH1A1 (1:100), goat anti SOX10 (1:1000), rabbit anti CPE (1:200), goat anti CALB2 (1:1000). Secondary antibodies used were: Goat anti Rabbit Alexa Fluor 488 (1:500), Donkey anti Rabbit Alexa Fluor 488 (1:500), Donkey anti Human Alexa Fluor 594 (1:500), Donkey anti Chicken Alexa Fluor 647 (1:500), and Donkey anti Rabbit Alexa Fluor 405 (1:500).

#### Glia and neuron quantification

#### Tacr3tdTomato whole-mount quantifications

10–15 maximum intensity projections of 50 μm Z-stacks were taken at 20x magnification covering a 430 × 430 μm region each, randomly sampling both ileum and distal colon from male and female mice at weaning and adulthood. Whole-mount samples were then flipped and 10–15 maximum intensity projections of 100 μm Z-stacks of the mucosa were taken. For quantification of Tacr3 reporter expression in enteric neurons and glia in Figures 2E, 2F, S2F, and S2G, the % of Tacr3+ cells are reported as the proportions of S100B+ glia or ANNA-1+ neurons that were tdTomato+ in each anatomically defined compartment (as depicted in magnified view of S100B+ [cyan] cells in Figure 2E that is shown in Figure S2F). We classified ‘‘connective’’ glia as those which had cell somas entirely within fiber tracts between ganglia and were not touching any neuronal somas. The dashed line in Figure S2F indicates the boundary between intraganglionic and connective glia in this representative image. Intramuscular glia (example denoted with an asterisk in the panel) reside in the muscularis outside ganglia and the connectives between ganglia. Quantifications were conducted manually using the Cell Counter plugin on ImageJ.

For P1-P14 ages, ileum and mid to distal colon from Tacr3iRESCre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice were analyzed. P1 and P7 tissues were mounted as tubes, while P14 tissue was cut open along the mesenteric border and pinned flat for fixation and staining, similar to tissues from adult mice. For quantification of the developmental emergence of Tacr3+ glia in the myenteric plexus (Figure 5B), at ages P1 and P7 when enteric ganglia are less distinct, the proportion of Tacr3+ glia are reported as the fraction of all S100B+ cells in the imaging fields that were tdTomato+. For P14 and P21, when enteric ganglia are distinct and connected by bridging fiber bundles, the proportion of Tacr3+ glia is reported as the fraction of all S100B+cells within myenteric ganglia that were tdTomato+.

#### Postnatal TACR3 inhibitor experiments and analysis of tissue from Tac2 KO mice

10–15 maximum intensity projections of 50 μm Z-stacks were taken at 20x magnification (422.13 × 422.13 μm field size) of the muscularis for drug- and vehicle-treated mice using the same imaging conditions. Z-stacks were taken from the myenteric plexus through the submucosal plexus. Whole-mount samples were then flipped and 10–15 maximum intensity projections of 100 μm Z-stacks of the mucosa were taken. Intramuscular glia were counted from maximum projection images of the Z-stack stopping at the 2 μm plane before the submucosal plexus emerged. Quantifications were manually conducted using the Cell Counter plugin on ImageJ.

#### Neuronal quantification in Tac2Cre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ intestinal segments

Following whole-mount immunostaining for the pan-neuronal marker anti-ANNA-1, twenty Z-stack images were taken from each distal ileum and colon segment of Tac2Cre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ male and female mice. Field size and thickness of Z-stacks were the same as described for Tacr3tdTomato whole-mount quantifications. Images were acquired by random sampling of fields in each tissue segment. Quantifications were manually conducted using the Cell Counter plugin on ImageJ to count ANNA-1+ tdTomato+ neurons in each field.

#### Quantitative RT-PCR (qPCR)

For validation of bulk RNA-seq results, ileal muscle and mucosa were stripped from CD1, Plp1CreERT2 Rosa26DTA/+ mice, or their Cre-negative Rosa26DTA/+ littermate controls and immediately placed in Trizol reagent on dry ice. RNA was extracted using phenol/chloroform extraction methods followed by cleanup with the RNeasy Kit. RNA was converted to cDNA using the iScript cDNA Synthesis Kit and qPCR was performed with SYBR Select Master Mix using the oligonucleotide primer pairs (IDT) listed in the key resources table.

#### Preparation of cell suspensions and flow cytometry

For bulk RNA-seq, male and female 8–12-week-old Plp1eGFP mice were fasted for 1 h and then euthanized by cervical dislocation. Approximately 8 cm of the distal small intestine was removed and immediately submerged in chilled Hank’s Balanced Salt Solution (HBSS) with penicillin-streptomycin (100 U/mL). Fine forceps were used to gently slide the intestine onto a crochet needle, and a razor blade was used to make a small incision at the edge of the tissue. Then, a dry cotton swab was used to gently roll the muscle layer off the mucosa. For bulk RNA-seq, muscle was placed in digestion media (HEPES buffered saline 2X, 1.25 mM CaCl2, 2.9 mg/mL Dispase II, 1 mg/mL Collagenase A, 50 μg/mL DNAse I) in a 37°C water bath for 30 min, and triturated with a 5 mL pipette at the 15-min interval. Mucosal tissue was placed in chilled HBSS + 10 mM DTT for 5 min (vigorously shaken for the first 30 s) and then solution was decanted and tissue was washed quickly with chilled HBSS in a petri dish. Then, mucosal tissue was transferred to a 15 mL falcon tube with HBSS + 5 mM EDTA for 5 min to further remove epithelial cells. After the EDTA rinse, solution was removed and mucosal tissue was washed in HBSS in a petri dish. HBSS was removed and tissue was resuspended in 2 mL of pre-warmed digestion media, chopped more finely with scissors, and transferred back into a 15 mL falcon tube with 5 mL pre-heated digestion media in a 37°C water bath for 45 min. Tissue was triturated every 15 min. Following digestion, both mucosal and muscle tissue were spun down at 500 x g for 5 min at 4°C. Supernatant was removed, and pellet was resuspended in 5 mL of Trypsin-EDTA 0.25% phenol red and incubated for 5 min at 37°C. Trypsin digestion was inactivated with 10 mL of fetal bovine serum (FBS) and cells were spun down at 500 x g for 5 min. Supernatant was removed and muscle cells were resuspended in 5 mL chilled FACS buffer (2% FBS + PBS + 1 mM EDTA) and strained through a 70 μm cell filter into a 50 mL conical tube. Simultaneously, mucosal cells were resuspended in 2 mL of 0.1mg/mL DNAse in HBSS at 37°C for 10 min. Samples were then spun down at 500 x g, and muscularis cells were resuspended in ∼250 μL FACS buffer + 1 μg/mL propidium iodide for sorting. Mucosal cells were resuspended in 5 mL FACS buffer and strained through a 100 μm filter and spun down at 500 x g for 5 min prior to resuspending in 500 μL of FACS buffer + 1 μg/mL propidium iodide. A SH800S SONY sorter with an 130 μm nozzle was used to isolate ∼10,000 single GFP+ and GFP− cells from muscle or mucosa per mouse into 525 μL of pre-chilled RLT lysis buffer + 7.5 mM TCEP. RNA was extracted and purified immediately using RNAeasy Micro kit and stored at −80°C until library preparation. Of note, in this method of mechanical tissue preparation, some but not all submucosal ganglia segregated into the muscularis compartment.

For single-cell RNA sequencing, 3 male Plp1eGFP Tacr3IRES-Cre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+mice at P21 were used. The entire small intestine (minus duodenum) was removed from each animal, the muscularis layer was mechanically isolated and digested as above for sorting. A BD FACS Melody sorter with a 100-μm sort nozzle was used to isolate GFP+ cells directly into a 24-well plate with chilled DMEM. Isolated cells were resuspended in a 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tube with sterile PBS + 2% FBS prior to analysis and loading into the 10X controller.

#### RNA sequencing and bioinformatic analyses

#### Bulk RNA sequencing

24 mucosal and muscularis RNA samples passed RIN quality scores >7 on the Agilent Pico Bioanalyzer and were submitted for library preparation and sequencing at the Harvard Biopolymers core facility. mRNA pull-down and cDNA synthesis were performed using Takara SMARTseq v4 kit, followed by library prep using the Illumina NexteraXT kit. Paired end sequencing was then performed using Novaseq 6000 with an average read count of ∼50–75 million reads per sample and an average of 90% mapped reads to the genome and minimum ∼50% reads aligned to exons as determined using Qualimap. FASTQ files were converted into BAM files and aligned to the mouse genome GRCm39 using STAR 2.5.2 on O2 high performance computing cluster through Harvard Medical School. Samtools flagstats was used to compute alignment efficiency of reads. Count files were generated using Subread 2.0.0 package and FeatureCounts for all samples. Subsequent count matrix generation, differential analyses, and visualization of sequencing data were performed using R 4.3.1 DESeq2 and ggplot2 packages. Of the 24 samples, 19 were used for downstream analysis because PCA and Pearson correlation showed clear segregation of these samples into mucosal and muscularis GFP+ and GFP-populations. 5 of the 24 samples were not used for downstream analysis due to suspicion for incomplete separation of tissue layers: 1 female GFP+ and GFP− muscle samples that clustered with mucosal samples, 2 male mucosal GFP+ and 1 female mucosal GFP+ that clustered with muscle samples.

#### Graphical visualizations

Venn diagrams for shared gene programs were generated using both Venny (https://bioinfogp.cnb.csic.es/tools/venny/) and BioRender. Schematics were generated in Keynote and BioRender. Volcano plots of differential analyses conducted were obtained using the EnhancedVolcano package in R.

#### BayesPrism deconvolution

Cell type and gene expression deconvolution66 was conducted on mucosal glia using a cell signature gene expression matrix extracted from the Smillie et al. single-cell sequencing dataset of mucosal cells from human mucosal biopsies.28

#### Macrophage computation correction

To correct for overrepresentation of macrophage signatures in the mucosal glial dataset, single sample gene set enrichment scores (ssGSEA) were computed for each mucosal GFP+ and GFP− sample using the singscore package in R https://bioconductor.org/packages/singscore. Scores were calculated based on coordinated gene expression of macrophage genes Cx3cr1, Adgre1, and Mpeg1. The vector of enrichment scores was then included as a covariate while performing differential analysis. This analysis was only performed in the mucosal dataset, as macrophage enrichment was not a dominant signature in the muscularis samples.

#### Gene set enrichment analyses (GSEA)

Gene set enrichment was conducted using both web-based g:Profiler (https://biit.cs.ut.ee/gprofiler/gost) and the Broad Institute GSEA software (GSEA.app 4.3.2). Analyses for bulk sequencing were conducted using the macrophage-corrected signature for mucosal glia compared to mucosal GFP-negative controls and unmodified signature for muscularis glia compared to muscularis GFP-negative controls. Gene set enrichment of single-cell glial dataset transcriptomes in mucosal and muscularis glial cells was reported based on comparing normalized enrichment scores (NES) for each population. For signatures that had no enrichment, NES value of 0 was designated. Single cell transcriptomes from published datasets were generated from extracting cluster markers for each major glial type. For PNS glia (1,552 satellite glia, 1,733 Schwann cells from naive, uninjured condition),24 data were downloaded and re-analyzed from GEO: GSE154659. For CNS glia (19,377 astrocytes, 30,253 oligodendrocytes, 5,425 microglia),12 data was downloaded as a loom file from http://mousebrain.org/adolescent/downloads.html and converted to a Seurat object for analysis.

#### Single-cell RNA sequencing

Single cell suspensions of GFP+ muscularis cells were stained with trypan blue to assess viability and cell concentration. Approximately 4,000 cells per sample were then loaded onto the 10X Chromium controller. Libraries were prepared according to the manufacturer’s protocols (Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3’ Reagent Kit v3.1 and dual index). Samples were pooled 1:1 prior to sequencing using the Illumina NextSeq 500 150 cycle kit. Read depth was calculated using CellRanger and was ∼16,000 reads per cell. Single cell analyses were conducted using Seurat 4.3.0 and subpackages. Color palettes from scCustomize were used in FeaturePlot. Clustering was performed using the default Seurat Louvain algorithm and a resolution of .35, as determined using the Clustree package.

#### In situ hybridization (RNAscope)

Intestinal tissue was rapidly dissected into ice-cold PBS + 4 mM ribonucleoside vanadyl complexes (RVC) to inhibit RNAse activity and flushed to remove fecal contents. Segments of ∼2 cm were fixed in RNAase-free 4%PFA/PBS for 24 h and then incubated for 24 h in 30% sucrose rocking at 4°C. Tissue was embedded in pre-chilled molds containing OCT compound, frozen on dry ice, and stored at −80°C until cryosectioning. Tissue blocks were equilibrated at −20°C for 30 min prior to sectioning. 8-μm slices were collected onto glass slides and stored at −20°C for 16–24 h before performing RNAscope. RNAscope V2 kit from ACD Bio was used for performing in situ hybridization. The slides were air-dried for 1–2 h in the cryostat at −20°C, washed in RNAase-free PBS for 3 × 5 min, and baked for 30 min at 60°C. They were post-fixed with pre-chilled 4% PFA (made fresh from electron microscopy-grade 16% PFA) for 15 min at 4°C and dehydrated in increasing concentrations of ethanol (50%, 70%, and twice 100% for 5 min each). The slides were then treated with hydrogen peroxide for 10 min at RT and washed in DEPC-treated water. For antigen retrieval, slides were immersed in Target Retrieval Reagent pre-heated to 99°C in an Oster steamer for 5 min. Following a wash in DEPC-treated water at RT, they were incubated in 100% ethanol for 3 min at RT, dried, and subjected to RNAscope Protease III treatment for 30 min at 40°C in an RNAscope hybridization oven. After two washes with PBS (10X PBS diluted in DEPC-treated water), probe hybridization and signal amplification were carried out per manufacturer’s protocol for RNAscope V2. Probes used: Tacr3-C1, Sox10-C3, Pappa-C2, Sfrp1-C2, Csf1r-C1, Cd300a-C1, Mpeg1-C1, Adgre1-C2, Tarm1-C1, Cdh19-C1. Opal dye 570, Opal dye 690, and Opal dye 520 were used for fluorescent labeling. Post-RNAscope IHC was performed as described above. Slides were then mounted with Vectashield containing DAPI (Vector Labs Cat# H-1200–10).

#### Quantification of mucosal macrophage and glial transcript expression

To label glial cells, 5-week-old male and female Plp1CreERT2 Rosa26tdTomato/+ Cx3cr1GFP/+ mice were administered 8 mg tamoxifen (Toronto Research Chemicals T006000) dissolved in corn oil once via orogastric gavage. Tissue was collected at 11 days post-tamoxifen and processed immediately for RNAscope as described above. High magnification images of 289 TdTomato+ glia and 518 GFP+ macrophages were manually counted and labeled as either ‘‘expressing’’ or ‘‘non-expressing’’ RNA transcripts based on the presence of fluorescent RNAscope puncta localizing to the nucleus of the cells. Due to proximity of macrophages and glia in the lamina propria, only transcripts detected clearly in the nucleus were included and RNA puncta in processes were excluded to maximize stringency and avoid misassigning transcript expression.

#### Testing effects of TACR3 inhibition on glial populations

For developmental inhibition, hemizygous Plp1eGFP and wild-type littermate mice were administered once daily subcutaneous injections of 5mg/kg TACR3 antagonist SB2222–00 or vehicle (10% DMSO in corn oil) for 7 days from P14 to P20. For adult inhibition, wild-type CD1 mice were administered SB2222–00 or vehicle daily as above from P56-P62. On the 7th day, mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation 2 h post-injection and intestinal tissue was harvested for RNA and IHC analyses.

#### Gastrointestinal transit time and fecal pellet output assays

Motility assays for total transit time, stool water, and fecal pellet output were all performed in the morning at 9 am. Total gastrointestinal transit time was performed as previously described.18 In brief, individual mice were placed in empty cages with ad libitum food and water, and administered 300 μL 6% carmine red solution (in 0.9% NaCl) at 9 am by orogastric gavage. 30-min and 60-min fecal pellet output measurements were collected for each mouse over the subsequent hour. Then, starting at 10 am, stools were monitored every 10 min until expulsion of first red pellet, which was recorded as total GI transit time.

For assessments of TACR3 agonism or antagonism on GI motility, male and female CD1 mice were habituated in the mouse facility for 1–2 weeks. On day of testing, mice were placed in individual cages, administered a single dose of fezolinetant 10 mg/kg, senktide 5 mg/kg, or vehicle by intraperitoneal injection at 8:30 am and then gavaged with carmine red 30 min later. Cross-over studies were conducted for females to account for variability. Fezolinetant and senktide were freshly resuspended in vehicle (10% DMSO in corn oil) on experimental days.

#### Ex vivo calcium imaging of colonic explants

Following euthanasia by cervical dislocation, a ventral midline incision was made and the entire colon was removed and placed in a Sylgard (Dow-Corning, Midland, MI, USA)-lined 6 cm dish. The contents of the colon were gently flushed, and then the middle region of colon was split and pinned flat, mucosa-side down, to a width of 6–6.5 mm. A region of the colon was also opened at the distal end and pinned flat, serosa-side down. Multiple small brush strokes were applied with india ink to provide a fiducial mark for movement subtraction. The tissue was perfused at 6 mL/min with Krebs–Ringer buffer (KRB; composition (mM): NaCl: 118; KCl: 4.7; NaHCO3: 25; MgCl2: 1.2; NaH2PO4: 1.2; glucose: 11; CaCl2: 2.5; pH: 7.4; 21°C) that was gassed with 95% O2, and 5% CO2 and heated before the dish by a temperature controller (TC-344C; Warner Instruments, Hamden, CT, USA) to 35–37°C. For mucosal stimulation, 30 s into the 2-min video, 5 brush strokes were applied to the distal mucosa over the course of 5 s. Ca2+ imaging recordings (2-min videos) were performed on a Nikon FN-1 upright microscope with a 20X Fluor water-immersion lens. Tissue was illuminated with a Spectra X light engine (Lumencor, Beaverton, OR, USA). Image sequences were captured using a Prime 95B Camera (Photometrics, Tuscon, AZ, USA) and a Windows-based PC using Nikon NIS Elements 4.1. Image sequences were recorded at 20 frames per second and exported as 16-bit TIFF files into custom-written software (Volumetry G8d67). An ROI was placed over a fleck of india ink that stayed within focus during the entire movie, and this was captured as a track and used to measure the displacement of the tissue. This displacement track was then used as a template to subtract the motion that occurred during the contraction so that the onset and duration of Ca2+ responses in enteric glia could be captured and compared with those of the movement. Background and region of interest (ROI) responses were calculated as spatial maps of the standard deviation (SD) of fluorescence intensity (SD maps) from beginning to end of each video as previously described.68 Background-subtracted spatial maps of fluorescence were color-coded using a ‘‘Fire’’ color lookup table (LUT). Background-subtracted traces of fluorescence intensity in 16-bit intensity units (iu16) were normalized to a starting value of 1 and then plotted as fluorescence divided by initial fluorescence values (F/F0). ‘‘Response %’’ represents the percentage of each glial type that exhibited a Ca2+ response to mucosal stimulation over the denominator that exhibited a response to KCl at the end of the experiment. ‘‘Amplitude’’ represents the peak fluorescence amplitude over initial (F/F0) and ‘‘duration’’ indicates the length of Ca2+ responses. ‘‘Onset’’ represents the onset of the glial Ca2+ response relative to contraction onset. Fezolinetant was perfused in heated, oxygenated KRB for at least 15 min before videos were obtained in response to distal mucosal stimulation. Senktide and potassium chloride (KCl) were bath applied. Stock concentrations of senktide and fezolinetant were each dissolved in a concentration of DMSO (0.1%) that does not induce or affect mucosal stimulation-induced glial Ca2+ responses on its own.

#### Ex vivo analysis of colonic motor behaviors

For imaging colonic motility, the colon distal to the cecum was acutely isolated from adult wild-type CD1 mice and cannulated in an organ bath maintained at 37°C containing continuously oxygenated Krebs solution (see schematic in Figure S4G). The organ bath accommodates two colons, and colons from experimental (1 μM fezolinentant) and control (vehicle) conditions were studied in tandem in every recording session. Intraluminal pressure was kept consistent between both colons and across experiments by regulating fluid column heights leading to both cannulae. After a 30-min equilibration period, colonic contractile activity was video recorded and analyzed using Scribble and Matlab scripts, as previously described.8 In brief, this analysis generates spatiotemporal heat maps from each 15-min video in which color represents gut width (degree of contraction), the X-axis represents the proximal-to-distal length of the colon, and the Y-axis represents time. Colonic migrating motor contractions (CMMCs) were defined as contractions that originated in the proximal colon and successfully propagated at least 50% of the length of the tissue. Two 15-min videos were analyzed per each of 8 mice per condition.

#### Testing association of TAC3 and TACR3 genetic variants with stool consistency

Stool consistency was studied based on questionnaire data from UKB, a large population-based cohort of approximately 500,000 participants recruited in the United Kingdom.69 Hard stool (UKB datafield ID 21033) was studied as a quantitative trait in relation to the question ‘‘In the last 3 months, how often did you have hard or lumpy stools?’’ from the DHQ questionnaire. Individuals of European ancestry (pan.ukbb.broadinstitute.org/docs/qc; N = 153,185; 60.4% female) and with no excess heterozygosity or missing genotypes (UKB data field 22027) were included in the analyses. UKB has approval from the North West Multi-centre Research Ethics Committee as a Research Tissue Bank, and this study was performed accessing data under application number 17435. SNPs located within the TAC3 and TACR3 loci spanning the respective coding sequences plus 2 kbp upstream and downstream were tested for association with hard stool using an additive linear mixed model (data extracted from genome-wide association study using REGENIE)70 adjusting for age, sex, top principal components and genotyping array. Finally, the effect of the SNPs on TAC3 gene expression (eQTLs) across human tissues was evaluated using publicly available data retrieved from the GTEx portal.71

### QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS

Both R 4.2.0 and Prism were used for statistical analyses and graphical visualization. Bar graphs in Figures 2, 3, 5, 6, S2, S4, S6, and S7 show individual data points and means with error bars denoting standard errors of the mean (SEM). For Tacr3IRESCre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ glia and neuron quantifications in Figure 2, two-way ANOVA with Šidák’s multiple comparisons test was performed to compare glial compartments or neuron compartments within ileum and colon separately. For intestinal motility, fecal pellet output, and CMMC experiments, paired or unpaired t tests were conducted comparing drug to vehicle for each sex separately, as noted in the figure legends. For quantifications of glial responses in calcium imaging experiments in Figure 3, unpaired t tests were used to compare mean responses between vehicle and drug-exposed glia of each type. For developmental Tacr3IRESCre/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ quantifications in Figure 5, one-way ANOVA was used across developmental time points for ileum and mid/distal colon. For analysis of sex differences during development, two-way ANOVA with Šidák’s multiple comparisons tests were performed. For developmental inhibitor and Tac2 KO quantification analyses of glial populations in Figures 5 and 6, two-way ANOVA was performed comparing inhibitor versus vehicle or KO versus WT effect per glial or neuronal compartment. Sample size (n) for each experiment and what ‘‘n’’ represents (mice, cells, etc.) can be found in the relevant portion of the results section and/or the respective figure legend.

eLife Assessment

This study presents important findings on the function of enteric glia expressing proteolipid protein 1 (PLP1+ glia). The evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid, although the inclusion of additional data showing the mechanisms by which PLP1+ enteric glia acts on Paneth cells would have strengthened the study. The work will be of interest to colleagues studying intestinal biology.

## Abstract

Glial cells of the enteric nervous system (ENS) interact closely with the intestinal epithelium and secrete signals that influence epithelial cell proliferation and barrier formation in vitro. Whether these interactions are important in vivo, however, is unclear because previous studies reached conflicting conclusions [1]. To better define the roles of enteric glia in steady state regulation of the intestinal epithelium, we characterized the glia in closest proximity to epithelial cells and found that the majority express PLP1 in both mice and humans. To test their functions using an unbiased approach, we genetically depleted PLP1+ cells in mice and transcriptionally profiled the small and large intestines. Surprisingly, glial loss had minimal effects on transcriptional programs and the few identified changes varied along the gastrointestinal tract. In the ileum, where enteric glia had been considered most essential for epithelial integrity, glial depletion did not drastically alter epithelial gene expression but caused a modest enrichment in signatures of Paneth cells, a secretory cell type important for innate immunity. In the absence of PLP1+ glia, Paneth cell number was intact, but a subset appeared abnormal with irregular and heterogenous cytoplasmic granules, suggesting a

## Introduction

The intestinal epithelium is an important interface between an animal and its external environment, not just as a physical barrier but also as a dynamic regulator of digestion, energy balance, and mucosal immunity. The ENS, the intrinsic nervous system of the digestive tract, directs many intestinal epithelial functions. Glia are major cellular components of the ENS distributed throughout the radial axis of the intestine, from the muscular outer walls to the inner mucosal layer containing the epithelium. Most studies of enteric glia have focused on the cells which closely associate with neuronal soma in the myenteric plexus and have uncovered numerous roles for these glia in the regulation of neuronal functions in both health and disease [2     ], [3     ]. Many enteric glia, however, are located outside the myenteric plexus in the mucosa where they closely appose intestinal epithelial cells [4     ]–[8     ], raising the possibility that mucosal glia directly regulate epithelial cell functions.

Several enteric glia-derived cues, ranging from small molecules to growth factors, can alter epithelial cell proliferation and cell-cell adhesion in vitro (reviewed in [1     ]), supporting the possibility of glial-epithelial interactions. In the intestine, however, none of these factors are made exclusively by glia [1     ]. Moreover, studies in which enteric glia were depleted or disrupted in vivo have reported conflicting findings in terms of epithelial effects. For example, chemical gliotoxins do not cause major epithelial deficits [9     ], [10     ]. In contrast, a chemical-genetic model using a human GFAP promoter fragment to target glia in mice showed profound epithelial barrier defects and fulminant inflammation specifically in the distal small intestine [11     ]. Subsequent studies by multiple groups using more targeted systems to deplete or functionally disrupt glia defined by Plp1, Sox10, or Gfap expression, however, have not supported this finding. They found no major defects in epithelial properties at steady state or increased vulnerability to inflammation upon glial disruption even though all of these models exhibited deficits in other ENS-regulated functions, such as motility [12     ]–[15     ]. One study reported that simultaneous depletion of Plp1- and Gfap-expressing populations could provoke intestinal inflammation, implicating a subset of glia with particularly high Gfap transcript expression in the regulation of epithelial turnover through the secretion of Wnt proteins [15     ]. Genetic disruption of Wnt secretion in Gfap+ cells, however, affected epithelial turnover only upon radiation injury [15     ]. Thus, it largely remains unclear what, if any, epithelial functions enteric glia are necessary for in vivo at steady state.

To better delineate the functional significance of enteric glial-epithelial interactions in homeostasis, first we characterized the molecular phenotype of mucosal glia along the crypt-villus axis in both mice and humans. We found that Plp1 was the most widely expressed marker of mucosal glia in both species, supporting the use of its promoter to probe glial functions in vivo. Then, to interrogate glial functions in an unbiased way, we depleted Plp1+ cells in mice and examined gene expression along the longitudinal axis of the intestine. Surprisingly, glial loss had minimal effects on the intestinal transcriptome or the cellular composition of the epithelium. Targeting Plp1+ cells, however, caused a specific defect in Paneth cells leading to enriched gene expression signatures, diminished antimicrobial peptide secretion, and altered gut microbial composition. These observations uncover a link between enteric glia and Paneth cells and establish a role for enteric glia in regulating epithelial function in the healthy intestine in vivo.

## Results

## Plp1 expression broadly marks glia in the gut mucosa

Enteric glia, like Schwann cells in the periphery, are neural crest-derived and have been identified within tissues by molecular markers including Sox10, Gfap, Plp1, and S100b. Although most glia within enteric ganglia are labeled by these markers, heterogeneity in their expression has been reported [16     ], [17     ], particularly in glia located outside the myenteric plexus [18     ]. To determine which marker is most broadly expressed by mucosal glia and would thus be most useful for genetic interrogation of glial-epithelial interactions, we analyzed publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) datasets of human and mouse intestinal mucosa.

In human small and large intestines, expression of SOX10 and PLP1 was restricted to cluster of cells with a glial signature (Fig. 1A     , Supp. Fig. 1A-B     ). S100B was highly expressed by cells in this cluster but also detected in non-glial cells including macrophages and monocytes; GFAP was overall undetectable (Fig. 1A     , Supp. Fig. 1A-B     ). To validate these findings, we examined expression of the corresponding proteins by immunohistochemistry (IHC) in the human small intestine and found SOX10-, PLP1-, and S100B-immunoreactive cells in three compartments along the radial axis: the mucosa, enteric ganglia in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses, as well as intramuscular glia in the muscularis externa (Supp. Fig. 2A-B     , D     ). GFAP-immunoreactive cells were readily found within enteric ganglia but were rare in the mucosa (Supp. Fig. 2C     ). These observations are consistent with a recent study that examined SOX10, GFAP, and S100B by IHC in the human colon and found little to no GFAP, but robust SOX10 and S100B expression across all three compartments [19     ]. In the small intestine of patients with Crohn’s disease, a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), SOX10, PLP1, and S100B transcripts were highly enriched in mucosal glia while GFAP was enriched in various non-glial cells including fibroblasts and immune cells (Fig. 1B     ). In sum, SOX10, PLP1 and S100B are broadly expressed by human enteric glia across the radial axis of the gut, including mucosal glia, in both healthy and inflamed states, with SOX10 and PLP1 exhibiting the most cell type specificity.

In mice, we previously showed that PLP1 is widely expressed by enteric glia across the radial axis of the small and large intestines where its expression largely overlaps with S100B; a more limited subset expresses GFAP [18     ]. Consistent with these observations, analysis of scRNAseq data from the mouse colonic mucosa showed that Plp1 is broadly expressed across the single putative cluster of mucosal glia; Gfap, S100b, and Sox10 are also detectable in this cluster to variable extents (Supp. Fig. 1C     ). Given recent observations that a subset of Gfaphigh/Plp1low mucosal glia might be particularly important for epithelial regulation in the mouse small intestine [15     ], we closely compared Plp1 and Gfap expression in the mouse ileum. We performed whole-mount IHC for GFAP in Plp1-eGFP reporter mice to ensure the detection of colocalization despite any potential differences in subcellular distribution. Previous work from our lab and others has validated that eGFP expression in this reporter strain faithfully mirrors endogenous PLP1 expression within the enteric and central nervous systems [18     ], [25     ]. In adult Plp1-eGFP mice, we found that mucosal glia diverged sharply in terms of marker expression based on their location along the crypt-villus axis. While the majority of villus Plp1+ cells co-expressed GFAP, virtually none of the crypt-associated Plp1+ cells did so (Fig. 1C-D     ). With rare exceptions in some villi, GFAPimmunoreactive cells that did not express Plp1 were largely undetectable. Together, these observations indicate that Plp1 expression broadly marks enteric glia in mouse and human tissues and is among the most sensitive and specific markers for glia in the gut mucosa.
